answer.rationale: With the contract expiring in 14 days and the line running at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, switching vendors (memory_c2) or adding a second source (memory_c3) both carry onboarding/integration risk that could jeopardize delivery continuity right when there's no slack to absorb disruption. Deferring (memory_c5) is unattractive because the contract does not auto-renew and finance has mandated an 18% spend cut this cycle, so budget flexibility isn't the binding constraint. Renewing as-is (memory_c1) preserves stability but leaves the cost mandate unaddressed. Negotiating terms with the incumbent (memory_c4, reinforced by memory_c6's multi-year volume pricing pattern) offers a path to recover margin and possibly extend to a longer-term commitment for better unit cost, without introducing migration risk or single-source exposure, which best satisfies 'minimize TCO without increasing delivery risk.' I want to verify memory_c4 specifically since it's the load-bearing precedent for this action, to confirm the original record actually shows renegotiation achieved material savings (not just anecdotal) before committing the cycle's one decision to it. I'm flagging downstream risk because negotiation alone may not fully close an 18% gap, and I'm preserving uncertainty since the consolidated memory summaries may understate variance in outcomes across different renegotiation cycles.
